senses.gloss:
Rājā Rāmmohan Roy
------------------------------------------
Rājā Rāmmohan Roy (A. D. 1772-1833), the founder of the Brahma Samāj was born in a village in the Hoogly district of Bengal in 1772.
See BRAHMA-SAMĀJ.

Rājarājeśvarī
(‘the mistress of even the king of kings’)
------------------------------------------
The goddess of the Kailāsanātha temple at काञ्चीपुरम् in Tamil Nadu has been called राजराजेश्वरी, probably because the temple had been built by the king नरसिṁह Varma (the Second) (A. D. 695-722) who had assumed the title, ‘Rājarājeśvara,’ (the king of kings’).
The Lalitāsahasranāma (684) uses this name as one of the epithets of ललिता (Tripurasundarī). There, the name is interpreted as ‘one who is the mistress of even ब्रह्मा, विष्णु, महेश्वर and कुबेर’.
She is described elaborately in the works like the Ṣoḍaśīkalpa. The Bhairavī-tantra includes her among the Daśamahā-विद्यास् (ten aspects of the Divine मोथेर्). (See DAŚAMAHĀVIDYĀS for details.)
She is pictured as sitting on the left lap of शिव, on a throne with five deities (called ‘pretas’ here) (Brahmā, विष्णु, रुद्र, ईश्वर and सदाशिव) forming its legs as it were.
She is extremely beautiful and bright, but of red complexion. She has three eyes. The crescent मोओन् illumines her crown. The sun and full-मोओन् form her ear-rings. Her face is tranquil and pleasant. She is richly decorated with garlands and various kinds of jewels.
See also LALITĀ.

Rājamārttāṇḍa
------------------------------------------
See BHOJA.
King भोज of धारेश्वर wrote several works, out of which one was a वृत्ति (a brief commentary) on the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.). This has been named Rājamārttāṇḍa or Bhojavṛtti.
Sometimes another book of the same name is described as a work on अस्त्रोलोग्य् and धर्मशास्त्रस्; and, has been quoted by several later writers.

rājanīti
(‘policies of a king’)
------------------------------------------
See RĀJADHARMA.

Rājavidyā
(‘kingly or royal science’)
------------------------------------------
The ninth chapter of the Bhagavad-gītā is called Rājavidyā-rājaguhya-yoga.
It is called Rājavidyā since it is the राजा (king) of all विद्यास् (sciences).
See BHAGAVADGĪTĀ for details.

Rājarājeśvara
(reign A. D. 985-1014)
------------------------------------------
Rājarājeśvara I, was one of the greatest kings of South India. He was a conqueror, builder and administrator. The details of his conquests are known from his inscriptions.
It was he who built the बृहदीश्वर तेम्प्ले at Thanjavur (in Tamil Nadu).
See BṚHADĪŚVARA TEMPLE also.

Rājayoga
(‘the king of all yogas’)
------------------------------------------
The योग system of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) is generally known as राजयोग.
See YOGADARŚANA for details.

rājyāṅgas
(‘constituents of a State’)
------------------------------------------
According to the ancient and medieval works on political science or statecraft (Rājyaśāstra, Vārtā and दण्डनीति) like the Arthaśāstra of कौटिल्य (300 B. C.) the राज्याङ्गस् or the constituents of a State are six. They are: svāmin (king), mantripariṣad (council of ministers), जनपद (people), durga and बल (fort and armed forces), कोश (treasury), and मित्र (allies).
SVĀMIN (The king)
The ancient and medieval works on political science recognized the great necessity for the office of the king or the supreme Head of the State. Since everything concerning the State ultimately depended upon him, he was expected to possess some basic qualities and proficiency in some specified fields. They were: physical strength and stamina, expertise in the use of astras (missiles) and śastras (weapons) and a good knowledge of the four branches of learning viz., trayī (the वेदस्), आन्वीक्षिकी (logic), vārtā (economics and political science) and दण्डनीति (statecraft). To understand the basic principles of धर्म and act according to them he must have been properly educated, refined and cultured. Needless to say that self-control was an essential part of this training.
Since the stability of the society depended on the strict maintenance of धर्म by all concerned, and since the वर्ण-आश्रम-system was considered pivotal to it, the king was expected to enforce it strictly. In the process he was obliged to deal with the transgressors very sternly.
Contrary to the Western concept that the king was the owner of all the land over which he ruled, the Hindu धर्म-śāstras ordained that the land did not belong to him as he was only its trustee. However he could have a private property built up from the funds allotted to him in the management of the State. Consequently he could give gifts only from this!
The king had a fixed, but strenuous, daily routine. Sufficient time was allotted for all legitimate activities such as these: examining the income and expenditure position, preparing a balanced budget, tax-collections, planning welfare schemes for the people, consultations with the ministers, secret meeting with the spies bringing information, inspection of the armed forces and consultation with its officers, spending some time with the family members and personal prayers.
It goes without saying that always elaborate and strict arrangements were made for the personal safety of the king.
Kings who aspired to become empe-rors cherished a great desire to perform sacrifices like the राजसूय or अश्वमेध.
MANTRIPARIṢAD (Council of Ministers)
The ministry was usually in two tiers—the inner or core group and the outer, larger, council. The inner, the core, group comprised the crown-prince, the prime minister, the royal preceptor (rājaguru) and the commander-in-chief. All policy decisions and framing of laws were done by this inner group. The outer circle could consist of 8 to 23, or even more, persons. They were important officers and heads of departments. This outer circle was mainly concerned with the implementation of the decisions taken by the inner circle.
The king was expected not to go against the majority decisions.
JANAPADA (People)
Since the kingdom, the entire govern-mental system, is meant for the welfare of the people, they must be kept happy and contented. For this they need security and all opportunities for development. The primary means of achieving this is by giving them ड़ोओद्, clothing, shelter, health-care, एदुचतिओन् and avenues for employment. Hence, the king and his government must support and encourage all organizations of public service such as trade guilds, labour unions, educational institutions and self-government agencies like the pañcāyats. As far as possible, all welfare activities must be undertaken through them or with their cooperation.
DURGA AND BALA
(Forts and Armed Forces)
During those days, forts were extremely important for the defence system. They used to be built in important places, including the inaccessible ones, for emergencies. Vantage points were always preferred. They would have outer and inner structures, secret tunnels, proper places for the soldiers, weapons, treasury, ड़ोओद् and other essential commodities, and even secret places for hiding. ड़ोओद् and essential commodities were always kept in stock.
The espionage system was well-organized.
There were proper provisions and methods for the raising and training of the armed forces which consisted of four divisions: infantry, cavalry, chariot-force and elephant-force.
Since ship-building was well-known even in the early period, powerful navies formed part of the armed forces.
During wars and invasions, very strict rules were followed. A few of these are:
The soldiers should not fight with unarmed persons. Weak persons, women and children, sick people and refugees must never be harmed. No damage should be caused to agricultural fields and civilian industries. There should be no looting or molestation in the conquered territory. Local religions and customs must be honoured and never interfered with. Closest relative of the conquered king, if found fit, may be installed as the new king. He was to be a sāmanta (feudatory chief) paying tributes and supplying the army when the conquering king needs it. He had complete autonomy in all other respects.
People of the conquered country had to be befriended by proper means.
KOŚA (Treasury)
No activity of the State can be undertaken unless there is enough money and wealth to back it up. Hence, collection of taxes was a primary duty of the State.
The taxes levied were generally light or moderate, and never heavy. Land revenue was the main tax. Irrigation tax was also collected wherever irrigation had been provided. The tax was generally one-sixth or one-fifth of the produce. Arts, crafts and trades were also taxed. Reli-gious and educational institutions, disabled persons, unemployed people, साधुस् (recluses and मोन्क्स्) and ब्राह्मणस् (devoted to Vedic learning and an austere life) were exempted. During droughts, famines and other national emergencies taxes were either abolished or deferred.
Emergency funds were built up in a separate treasury and were never touched except in grave and critical situations. विद्यारण्य (A. D. 1350), the chief architect of the Vijayanagara Empire, is said to have built up an emergency treasury worth 920 million varahas (gold coins) and instructed the princes हरिहर and Bukka never to touch it except in extreme emergencies.">1
There was a constant and strict supervision of accounts. Tax-collectors were expected to behave humanely and invited severe punishments for cruelty.
The tax money was apportioned to various public purposes by proper budge-tary procedures.
MITRA (Ally)
For the consolidation of the State and help in emergencies, friends and allies were considered absolutely necessary. The first two of the four upāyas or means, viz., sāma (a spirit of reconciliation) and दान (the spirit of give and take), come in handy in this regard. (The other two—bheda [splitting the enemy ranks] and दण्ड [violent means including war]—were meant to be used against enemies and that too as a last resort.)
Potential enemies, when not amenable to sāma and दान, were to be neutralized.
Friendly countries were to be helped in their hour of need. Pacts signed were strictly honoured. There was to be no invasion on a king who was virtuous and was ruling according to धर्म!

rājadharma
(‘duties of a king)
------------------------------------------
The duties and the responsibilities of a king or the ruler of a country, have been delineated in great detail by the epics, the पुराणस् and the धर्मशास्त्रस्. Atrismṛti (28) summarises the whole topic in a superb, though succinct, manner thus: ‘The five duties of a king are: punishing the wicked, honouring the good, filling up the treasury by right means, meting out justice impartially and protecting the kingdom by all means at his disposal.’
Since the State depended heavily on the king, he was expected to possess some basic qualities and proficiency in some fields like physical strength and stamina, expertise in the use of weapons and missiles, and a good knowledge of econo-mics as also political science. A basic knowledge of the वेदस् and लोगिच् was also necessary.
It was his primary duty to see that all his subjects strictly followed the codes of वर्ण-आश्रम-धर्म. The transgressors were to be dealt with sternly.
The धर्मशास्त्रस् ordained that the land of the country was not his personal property, though he too could own some land and build up his private property by the funds of the State allotted to him for his maintenance.
The king had a fixed and strenuous daily routine. The legitimate activities prescribed were: examining the financial position of the State; tax-collections; preparing a balanced budget; planning welfare schemes for the people; consultation with the ministers and important officers; secret meetings with spies; inspection of armed forces and consultations with the commanders; and, finally, spending some time with the members of his own family.
Elaborate arrangements were made for the safety of the person of the king.
The Rājadharma section of the Mahābhārata (vide शान्तिपर्व, chs. 1 to 30) has elaborated the राजधर्म in great detail in 130 chapters.

rājarṣi
(‘a sagely king’)
------------------------------------------
A राजर्षि is a king who has risen to the state and stature of a ṛṣi or a sage, a person of spiritual wisdom. He has attained that state by dint of severe तपस् or austerity.
In ancient India, as a result of the एदुचतिओन् received in the gurukulas (forest academies run by well-known sages), even the princes were trained to become men of spiritual wisdom.
Certain kinds of विद्यास् (meditations) like the Pañcāgni Vidyā (‘the knowledge of the ड़िवे ड़िरेस्’, Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4-9) were the special prerogatives of these rājarṣis.
Janaka, अश्वपति Kekaya and प्रवाहण जैवलि were some of the rājarṣis.

rajas
------------------------------------------
See GUṆA and SĀṄKHYA DARŚANA.

rājā
(‘one who shines [with power]’ ‘king’)
------------------------------------------
Ancient Hindu scriptures recognised the great necessity for the office of the king or the Supreme Head of the State. Otherwise, jungle-law would prevail.
In the Vedic age, the kings were actually social leaders elected by the people. The office of the king as a hereditary institution, seems to be a later development. Even then, the people’s consent was taken before the appointment of the yuvarāja (the crown prince) who would later on succeed to the throne.
Most of the ancient kings traced their descent to सूर्य (the Sun), चन्द्र (the मोओन्), or अग्नि (the Fire).
See RĀJYĀṄGAS for more details.

Rājasūya
(‘to press out or generate a king’)
------------------------------------------
One of the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् mentioned often by the पुराणस्, the राजसूय (-याग), could be performed only by a क्षत्त्रिय or a king.
Some authorities opined that it could be performed after the वाजपेय (another well-known sacrifice) while others felt that it should be done before. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (9.3.4.8) declares that one who performs the राजसूय becomes a rājan (king) whereas the performer of the वाजपेय becomes a saṁrāṭ (emperor).
It is a rite of royal consecration and lasts for more than two years.
The yajamāna or the sacrificer has to take the दीक्षा or preliminary vows on Phālguna-śukla-pratipad (first day of the bright half of the month of Phālguna, generally in February/March). He then performs a सोम sacrifice called the पवित्र. The procedure for this is the same as for the अग्निष्टोम sacrifice. (See AGNIṢṬOMA for details.)
This is then followed by a series of iṣṭis (sacrifices performed with oblatory materials like ghee and porridge) like अनुमति, चातुर्मास्य, Apāmārgahoma (a rite to drive away demons) and so on.
The most important part of the राजसूय is the अभिषेचनीय rite (the rite of unction lasting for five days) wherein the water for the अभिषेक (the act of pouring the water on the head) has to be brought from seventeen sources, kept in seventeen vessels of udumbara wood (Ficus glomearata) and poured on the sacrificer’s (the king’s) head by several persons including the commoners.
Then there is a symbolic march for the plunder of cows. A group of one hundred cows is ‘seized’ by the king and then given back to their owners.
A dice-play in which the sacrificer-king always wins is also a part of the ritual.
As in other sacrifices, the sacrificer has to take the avabhṛthasnāna or the concluding bath.
The fees prescribed for this sacrifice is extremely heavy—2,40,000 cows, to the various priests.
The Pāṇḍavas are said to have performed this sacrifice in इन्द्रप्रस्थ, their capital (vide Mahābhārata, Sabhā-parva chs. 33-45).
